nature-eco-142.title: Conservation or preservation: use nature wisely, or leave it alone
nature-eco-142.text: In the early twentieth-century environmental movement, two camps formed. Conservationists wanted to regulate human use of nature. Preservationists wanted to remove human impact altogether. The split survives in the definitions: conservation seeks the proper use of nature, while preservation seeks to protect nature from use. C. Anne Claus draws a similar line between 'conservation-far', which protects nature by separating it from people, and 'conservation-near'.

nature-eco-143.title: Evidence-based conservation: testing what works
nature-eco-143.text: Conservation decisions that relied on intuition and experience had led to costly, poor outcomes. Evidence-based conservation answers this by basing decisions and policy on systematically assessed evidence. The idea borrows from evidence-based practice in medicine. The evidence includes peer-reviewed science, practitioners' experience, expert assessment, and local and Indigenous knowledge, along with economic factors.

nature-eco-141.title: For its own sake or for ours? Values in conservation
nature-eco-141.text: Why save a species: for its own sake, or for ours? Conservation rests on different values, from nature's worth in itself to its usefulness for human wellbeing. One view, described in {{ref:nature-val-060}}, gives that inner worth to individual organisms, while ecoholism values whole species or ecosystems. Utilitarian, human-centered conservation seeks a proper valuation of human impacts on nature, in terms of human wellbeing now and in the future. Some branches, such as compassionate conservation, focus on the welfare of sentient animals. How these values are weighed and traded among people sets the social and political limits on conservation.

nature-eco-092.title: Grazing or rainfall? The fight over what makes deserts
nature-eco-092.text: Early studies blamed livestock, naming overgrazing as a leading cause of desertification. Later work on the Sahel region of Africa shifted attention to climate. Drought there is now thought to stem mainly from rainfall swings driven by ocean temperatures, aerosols and greenhouse gases. Changing ocean temperatures and lower sulfate emissions re-greened the Sahel, leading some scholars to call vegetation loss from farming a minor factor. Even the word is slippery: by 2005 there were more than 100 formal definitions of desertification. Researchers still disagree on whether local overuse or climate variability is the main recent driver.

nature-eco-049.title: Forest fragmentation: islands of trees in a sea of fields
nature-eco-049.text: Remnant woodlands behave like islands of forest in a sea of fields and suburbs. Forest fragmentation is the form of {{ref:nature-nbs-115}} in which forests are reduced to small, isolated patches separated by farmland, open land or development. It is one of the greatest threats to forest biodiversity, especially in the tropics. The patches follow the principles of island biogeography: smaller or more isolated ones lose species faster than larger or better-connected ones.

nature-eco-048.title: Why small populations are genetically fragile
nature-eco-048.text: A population stranded in a habitat fragment often holds only part of the genetic diversity of the continuous habitat it came from. Fragmentation then reduces gene flow, the movement of genes as individuals migrate between populations. Small populations face linked genetic risks: lost variety, inbreeding and genetic drift. Drift, random change in a population's genetic makeup, matters more the smaller the population. Inbreeding lowers reproduction and survival and adds to extinction risk in endangered species.

nature-eco-061.title: How fertilizer hides worn-out land
nature-eco-061.text: On intensive farms, heavy use of fertilizers and other inputs can hide falling soil productivity while the underlying damage worsens. Farmers decide mainly on productivity and profit, so degradation on farms reflects local choices as well as global drivers such as trade and climate change. Compensating with inputs keeps yields high in the short term. It also brings diminishing returns, higher costs, acidification and pollution. Threshold effects, sudden shifts once a limit is passed, can eventually lead to land abandonment in long-farmed areas.

nature-nbs-156.title: Land degradation neutrality: a UN goal of no net loss
nature-nbs-156.text: Target 15.3 of the UN goals described in {{ref:nature-gov-010}} aims, by 2030, to combat desertification, restore degraded land and soil, and strive for a land degradation-neutral world. Land degradation neutrality is that goal: a world where degraded land is restored and degradation no longer advances. The UNCCD, the UN body against desertification, pursues it through its 2018-2030 Strategic Framework, alongside fighting desertification, land degradation and drought. The UN restoration decade described in {{ref:nature-nbs-137}} lists the target among the agreements restoration helps achieve. The economics are tricky. Restoring degraded land yields ecosystem services that benefit society at large, which makes it a collective-action problem of providing public goods.

nature-mkt-009.title: One big reserve or several small ones? The SLOSS debate
nature-mkt-009.text: Is it better to protect a single large reserve or several small ones of the same total area? Ecologists fought over this SLOSS question, short for "single large or several small", in the 1970s and 1980s. It grew out of {{ref:nature-eco-134}}. Many small forest islands typically cannot hold the biodiversity of one continuous forest, even with greater combined area. Yet a review of 381 significant effects of fragmentation itself found 76% positive and 24% negative, so several small patches can sometimes win. Where that holds, the approach in {{ref:nature-nbs-238}} could help species more than the one in {{ref:nature-nbs-237}}. Studies still disagree on whether fragmentation itself harms or helps species.

nature-eco-120.title: Genetic rescue: how eight Texas panthers saved Florida's
nature-eco-120.text: Eight panthers from Texas were added to Florida's declining, inbred panther population. Genetic variation rose, and the population began growing markedly faster. Genetic rescue is the attempt to make a struggling population more viable by adding genetic diversity to it. It answers the risks described in {{ref:nature-eco-048}}. Keeping genetic diversity high is an important part of efforts to rescue species.

nature-eco-119.title: Fields of clones: the danger of genetic uniformity
nature-eco-119.text: Ireland's nineteenth-century Great Famine was caused partly by sameness. Its potatoes were grown from pieces of one parent plant, which made them effectively clones, open to epidemic. Selective breeding has produced whole farms of nearly genetically identical crop plants. With so little genetic diversity, a disease that attacks one genetic variant can wipe out an entire crop.

nature-eco-121.title: Measuring genetic diversity: loci, alleles and heterozygosity
nature-eco-121.text: How varied are a population's genes? Geneticists answer with a few simple indicators. One is the share of polymorphic loci, the places in the genome where a gene comes in more than one version. Another is heterozygosity, how often individuals carry two different versions. Others count alleles, or gene versions, per locus, and nucleotide diversity, the variation in the DNA itself. Simulation software uses allele frequencies and population size to predict a population's future.

nature-eco-153.title: Wildlife crossings: bridges and tunnels for animals
nature-eco-153.text: Along the Trans-Canada Highway through Banff, six overpasses and 38 underpasses have cut wildlife collisions by 80%. Wildlife crossings are overpasses and underpasses that let animals cross roads, canals and other infrastructure safely. Species have preferences: at Banff, black bears and mountain lions favor the darker underpasses. Fencing often complements crossings to reduce road deaths. They are a practical piece of the wider idea in {{ref:nature-eco-152}}.

nature-eco-071.title: DAFOR: rating a plant with a single letter
nature-eco-071.text: A field ecologist can rate a species in a plot with one letter: Dominant, Abundant, Frequent, Occasional or Rare. That is the DAFOR scale. DAFOR and its cousin ACFOR are semi-quantitative ratings based on viewing an area of set size. They give rough estimates of abundance but are not exact or objective, so better methods should be used where available.

nature-eco-070.title: Species abundance distributions: a few common, many rare
nature-eco-070.text: In most collections, a few species make up most of the individuals. A species abundance distribution describes how common or rare each species is within an ecosystem. It is one of the most basic and widely used measurements in ecology, with many methods of analysis. Its usual lopsided shape echoes the pattern in {{ref:nature-eco-069}}.

nature-eco-104.title: Old relics and young species: two kinds of endemics
nature-eco-104.text: The ginkgo tree is a paleoendemic: a relic of a once-widespread group now confined to a small area. Neoendemics are the reverse, young species that have not yet spread beyond where they arose. Stebbins and Major introduced both terms in 1965 to describe California's endemics. A related measure, phylogenetic endemism, weights species by how evolutionarily distinct they are, not just how many are endemic. These choices matter. How endemism is categorized affects how hotspots are defined, and so where conservation money goes.

nature-eco-149.title: Species evenness: are species shared out fairly?
nature-eco-149.text: Two meadows each hold four butterfly species, so their richness is equal. In one, each species makes up 25% of the butterflies. In the other, a single species makes up 80%. The first meadow is more diverse, because its species are more even. Species evenness describes how equal the abundances of the species in a community are. Combined with species richness, it determines {{ref:nature-eco-147}}, a key measure of community structure. Abundances are estimated by area-based counts, distance methods or mark-and-recapture studies.

nature-eco-147.title: Species diversity: richness and evenness combined
nature-eco-147.text: Sample a larger area and diversity rises, simply because the sample includes more individuals and more varied environments. That is one trap in measuring species diversity: the number of different species in a community, often weighted by how evenly individuals are spread among them. The term can mean species richness, taxonomic or phylogenetic diversity, or species evenness. It is often expressed as the number of equally abundant species that would give the same average abundance as the data, an idea explained in {{ref:nature-eco-077}}. Researchers quantify it with indices such as richness and the Shannon and Simpson indices, whose values are not directly comparable. A sample usually underestimates the diversity of the whole population. So sampling effort must be standardized before comparisons are made.

nature-eco-076.title: Alpha diversity: variety within a single site
nature-eco-076.text: R. H. Whittaker split diversity into three scales, and alpha diversity is the local one: the average species diversity found within individual sites. In Whittaker's scheme, a landscape's total diversity, explained in {{ref:nature-eco-117}}, depends on alpha and on how much sites differ from one another, explained in {{ref:nature-eco-079}}. There is no consensus on the right spatial scale, so alpha can be measured for subunits of any size. Researchers often measure it with species richness or with the Shannon and Simpson indices.

nature-eco-137.title: How biodiversity is measured
nature-eco-137.text: Nobody knows which genes may prove useful, so keeping as many genes as possible is the best choice for conservation. That makes measuring biodiversity essential. The usual indicator is the number of taxa, groups such as species, found in an area over a period of time. Species richness and species evenness are worked out first, and species diversity combines the two. The Shannon and Simpson indices are the two most popular measures. Diversity can also be measured at different scales: alpha within a site, beta between sites and gamma across a region. Each measure suits a particular use of the data. A more economically defensible measure would preserve options for adaptation and future human use.

nature-eco-096.title: Does variety make ecosystems work better?
nature-eco-096.text: Do more species make an ecosystem work better? Research on the ecological effects of biodiversity asks how the variety of species and genes shapes the way a community functions. It has focused on productivity and stability. Productivity is usually measured as the total aboveground plant biomass in an area. More diverse communities appear to produce more biomass and to be more stable when disturbed. Many long-term studies in grassy habitats find that diversity enhances productivity, though results vary. Diversity in species' functional roles may predict productivity better than the number of species. Experiments disagree on whether diversity itself or the particular mix of species drives productivity, and on whether diversity resists invasion. The stakes are real. If diversity stabilizes ecosystems, losing species could feed back into further losses. Habitat fragmentation alters these relationships, and losses can continue two decades after it. Losing species also means losing potential foods, medicines, industrial products and tourism.

nature-eco-047.title: The rescue effect: neighbors that keep a population alive
nature-eco-047.text: A small, isolated population can be saved by newcomers. Immigrants from nearby populations keep it from dying out, and they recolonize patches where a species was lost. This is the rescue effect. Brown and Kodric-Brown first described it, and it is widely used in the study of metapopulations, networks of linked populations. Fragmentation can break the rescue. When fragments lie far apart, a declining population may receive no immigrants to save it.

nature-eco-068.title: When clearing forest cools the planet: the reflection effect
nature-eco-068.text: Large-scale clearing north of 50°N gives net global cooling, while clearing in the tropics produces substantial warming. Studies since the early 1990s show this split. The cause is reflected sunlight, the property explained in {{ref:nature-eco-006}}. Bare high-latitude ground is much more reflective than intact forest, so clearing it sends more sunlight back to space. Metrics that count only carbon miss this effect.

nature-eco-067.title: Fewer trees, less rain
nature-eco-067.text: A 2025 study estimated that deforestation caused about 74% of the decline in dry-season rainfall across the Brazilian Legal Amazon from 1985 to 2020. Trees release water vapor, as {{ref:nature-eco-226}} explains, so fewer trees mean less rain nearby. Less rain brings a hotter, drier climate, longer dry seasons, more fires and disrupted pollinators. Deforestation in the Congo is expected to cut regional rainfall by up to 8-10% by 2100.

nature-eco-145.title: Fighting poaching: cut supply or cut demand?
nature-eco-145.text: When rhinos went on the strictest list of the trade agreement in {{ref:nature-mkt-001}}, horn prices rose and poaching grew. Rhinos survived where protection on the ground was adequate. Anti-poaching efforts can target the supply of poached goods or the demand for them, and the economics differ. Supply-side remedies include stronger laws and rights to land for local communities. But scarcer goods cost more, and through the snob effect that can draw wealthy buyers, offsetting enforcement gains. Some evidence suggests cutting demand works better than ever more policing, though few demand campaigns measure their impact.

nature-eco-116.title: Flagship species: pandas and tigers as conservation ambassadors
nature-eco-116.text: The Bengal tiger, the giant panda, the black rhinoceros and the Asian elephant all serve as flagship species. A flagship is a popular species chosen as symbols to win public support and money for conserving nature in a place. The idea is essentially a marketing one, and it has drawbacks. Flagships can skew priorities toward charismatic species at the expense of more threatened, less appealing ones. Charisma alone does not prevent extinction. All ten of the most charismatic animal groups in a 2018 study are endangered. Flagships can also clash with local people, as with the Asian elephant where human–elephant conflict occurs, a problem called 'flagship mutiny'.

nature-eco-113.title: The Big Five: Earth's greatest extinctions
nature-eco-113.text: The Cretaceous–Paleogene event 66 million years ago removed about 75% of all species, including the non-avian dinosaurs. It is one of the Big Five, the five geological intervals of exceptional diversity loss identified by Jack Sepkoski and David Raup in 1982. The others are the Late Ordovician, Late Devonian, Permian–Triassic and Triassic–Jurassic extinctions. A 2021 study linked the Big Five with about 5.2 °C of warming. They may not form a separate class at all. They seem to be the largest of a fairly smooth continuum of extinction events.
